Exmouth.region: Exmouth and the East Devon coast
Exmouth.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the East Devon coast
s1loc: Exmouth runs a busy visitor economy as the start of the Jurassic Coast, the World Heritage shoreline that runs east toward Dorset. Orcombe Point, marked by the Geoneedle unveiled in 2002, opens the 95-mile stretch, while over two miles of golden sand sweep from the Exe estuary to the cliffs. The seafront, the marina at the former dock and the wide beach anchor the town as one of Devon's marquee seaside draws across the year.

The leisure and activity layer reaches across the estuary and the sand. The World of Country Life near Sandy Bay runs an all-weather family attraction with farm encounters, deer and vintage transport, while Exmouth Marina and the Exe estuary host paddleboarding, kayaking, windsurfing and sailing. Phear Park, the old Phear family grounds given to the town, adds tennis courts, a pitch-and-putt, a bowling green and a skate park, keeping activity operators busy through the warmer season.

Heritage and culture run deep here. A La Ronde, the curious sixteen-sided National Trust house built for two cousins in the 1790s, gives the town a distinctive landmark, while the Exmouth Pavilion, a 541-seat seafront theatre opposite the beach, stages shows through the year. The Georgian and Victorian terraces of the seafront, the old dock quarter now a marina and the events calendar across the town fill the diary along the East Devon coast.

Underpinning it all is a hotel, guest-house and self-catering trade serving the Jurassic Coast and the estuary, with a guide and boat-trip scene running across the Exe and along the cliffs. Exmouth station, the terminus of the Avocet Line, links the town to Exeter Central and St Davids for the main network, while the estuary ferry to Starcross and the cycle path toward Budleigh Salterton carry day-trippers heading along the wider East Devon shore.

Redcar.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Cleveland coast
s1loc: Redcar runs a traditional seaside visitor economy on the North Yorkshire and Cleveland coast, anchored by its long sandy beach and the Redcar Beacon, the striking spiral viewing tower on the seafront known locally as the vertical pier, which gives sweeping views over the bay. The esplanade, the wide promenade and the racecourse just back from the shore draw visitors across the year, with Coatham Beach and its dunes stretching north toward the river mouth.

The leisure and activity layer reaches along the shore and into the parks. The Coatham sands draw walkers, kitesurfers and horse riders, while Locke Park and Borough Park give families green space and play areas in the town. The seafront amusements, the beach and the wider Tees estuary nature sites keep activity operators and day-out trade busy through the warmer season, with surf and watersports drawing crowds to the open North Sea swells off the coast.

Heritage and culture run deep here. The Zetland Lifeboat Museum holds the oldest surviving lifeboat in the world, the Zetland of 1802, telling the story of the town's rescue tradition, while Kirkleatham Museum, set in a 1709 Queen Anne building that began as a free school, traces local industrial, maritime and social history. The conservation streets of old Coatham, the racecourse calendar and the events along the seafront add depth across the season.

Underpinning it all is a hotel, guest-house and holiday-let trade serving the coast, day-trippers and racegoers, with a guide and day-out scene built around the beach and the Cleveland hills. Redcar Central and Redcar East stations link the town along the Esk Valley and Tees lines to Middlesbrough and Saltburn, and the A174 carries visitors in, so operators handle stopover and seasonal trade as well as day-trippers heading for the North York Moors nearby.

Whitley Bay.region: Whitley Bay and the North Tyneside coast
Whitley Bay.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the North Tyneside coast
s1loc: Whitley Bay runs a thriving seaside visitor economy on the North Tyneside coast, anchored by the restored Spanish City, the white-domed Renaissance pleasure hall built in 1910 and reopened in 2018 as a dining and events centre after a seven-year restoration. The mile-long beach, Blue Flag-certified every year since 1994, sweeps the front, while the wider Links and promenade give the town a marquee seaside draw across the year along the open North Sea shore.

The leisure and activity layer reaches north along the coast. St Mary's Lighthouse, reached on a tidal causeway to St Mary's Island, dates from 1898 and rewards 137 steps with views over the nature reserve and bay, while the beach draws surfers, paddleboarders and year-round swimmers on the Atlantic swells. The Links, the dunes and the coastal paths toward Seaton Sluice give families and activity operators a busy outdoor offer through the warmer season along the front.

Heritage and culture run deep here. The Whitley Bay Playhouse, refurbished and reopened in 2009, stages theatre, music and comedy through the year, while the events along the promenade, the seafront festivals and the restored Spanish City complex give the town a strong cultural focus. The Victorian and Edwardian streets back from the seafront, the old Whitley Lodge and the events calendar across the front add depth beyond the modern beach offer along the Tyneside coast.

Underpinning it all is a hotel, guest-house and holiday-let trade serving the coast, day-trippers from Newcastle and weekend visitors, with a guide and day-out scene built around the beach and the lighthouse. Whitley Bay Metro station links the town directly into Newcastle and along the coast to Tynemouth and the city, and the A19 carries visitors in, so operators handle seasonal and stopover trade as well as day-trippers heading along the wider North Tyneside shore.

Houghton le Spring.region: Houghton-le-Spring and the City of Sunderland
Houghton le Spring.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the City of Sunderland
s1loc: Houghton-le-Spring carries a distinctive visitor economy on the southern edge of the City of Sunderland, dominated by Penshaw Monument, the great half-size replica of the Temple of Hephaestus in Athens built in 1844 in memory of John George Lambton, the first Earl of Durham. Set high on Penshaw Hill and a National Trust landmark visible for miles across Wearside, the monument anchors the area as a marquee day-out draw across the year.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Herrington Country Park, laid out across a former colliery site beside Penshaw Hill, with walking trails, an amphitheatre, a lake for angling, a children's playground and a skate park drawing families and walkers. Rainton Meadows nature reserve and the wider green spaces toward Rectory Park give activity operators and day-out trade a busy outdoor offer through the warmer season across the district below the monument.

Heritage and culture run deep here. The medieval Church of St Michael and All Angels, the resting place of the reformer Bernard Gilpin, the so-called Apostle of the North, anchors the historic town, while the annual Houghton Feast, one of the oldest fairs in the North East dating back centuries, fills the autumn calendar with rides, a fairground and an ox roast. The old town quarter and the events across the district add depth across the season.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and inn trade serving Sunderland, business visitors and day-trippers heading for the monument and the coast, with a guide and day-out scene built around Penshaw and Herrington. The A1(M) and A690 link the town to Sunderland, Durham and Chester-le-Street, and the nearby Metro and rail network carry visitors in, so operators handle stopover trade as well as day-trippers heading for the Wearside coast and the Durham countryside nearby.

Amesbury.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Stonehenge landscape
s1loc: Amesbury runs an outsized visitor economy for a small Wiltshire town, with Stonehenge, the greatest surviving megalithic monument in the British Isles and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986, standing within the parish two miles away and drawing over a million visitors a year. The English Heritage visitor centre, the standing stones on Salisbury Plain and the surrounding barrows and avenues anchor the town as a gateway to one of the most famous ancient landscapes on earth.

The leisure and activity layer reaches across the prehistoric downland and the river. Woodhenge, the neolithic timber circle a mile and a half from the town first traced from aerial photographs in 1925, and the Stonehenge Landscape trails run by the National Trust give walkers miles of open chalk country, while the River Avon winding through the town offers riverside walks, picnic spots and wildlife. The wider Salisbury Plain and the downs keep activity and day-out operators busy through the season.

Heritage and culture run deep here. Amesbury Abbey, a Benedictine house for women founded around 979 and later a great priory, gives the town a thousand years of monastic history, while the Church of St Mary and St Melor and the Ancestor sculpture at Solstice Park, marking ten thousand years of life in the area, add depth. The events tied to the solstice gatherings and the heritage calendar across the town fill the diary through the year.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and inn trade serving Stonehenge visitors, coach tours and day-trippers, with a deep tour-operator and guide scene running trips out to the stones from across the South and from London. The A303 carries vast seasonal traffic past the town, and Salisbury station nearby links the area to the main rail network, so operators handle heavy coach and stopover trade as well as visitors heading across the Wiltshire downs and Salisbury Plain.

Warwick.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Avon valley
s1loc: Warwick runs one of the Midlands' best-known visitor economies, dominated by Warwick Castle, the great medieval fortress founded by William the Conqueror in 1068 and now a major attraction with falconry displays, the trebuchet, the Mill and Engine House and shows staged through the season. Towering above the River Avon, the castle and its grounds draw vast crowds across the year and anchor the historic county town as a marquee day-out destination in Warwickshire.

The leisure and activity layer reaches along the river and the parks. The Hill Close Gardens, a rare survival of Victorian leisure plots restored as a heritage garden, and St Nicholas Park beside the Avon, with its riverside paths, boating and play areas, give families and activity operators a strong outdoor offer. The riverside meadows, the racecourse green and the trails toward the wider Avon valley keep day-out trade busy through the warmer season around the town.

Heritage and culture run deep here. The Lord Leycester Hospital, one of Europe's most important medieval timber-framed buildings, built by the guilds from 1380 beside the West Gate, sits alongside the Collegiate Church of St Mary, whose 130-foot tower and Beauchamp Chapel crown the town. The Market Hall Museum in its 17th-century building, the Georgian quarter rebuilt after the 1694 fire and the events calendar across the streets give Warwick a layered character through the year.

Underpinning it all is a deep hotel, inn and guest-house trade serving the castle, business travellers and visitors touring Shakespeare country, with a wide guide and tour scene built around the castle and the historic town. Warwick and Warwick Parkway stations link the town to Birmingham, London Marylebone and Stratford-upon-Avon, and the M40 carries day-trippers in, so operators handle heavy seasonal and stopover trade as well as visitors heading across the Avon valley and the wider Warwickshire countryside.

Erith.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Bexley riverside
s1loc: Erith runs a riverside visitor economy on the Thames in the London Borough of Bexley, anchored by Erith Pier, the longest pier in London, which reaches out into the river with wide views across the water and the marshes. Once Henry the Eighth's naval dockyard in the 16th century and a Victorian river-steamer resort, the town's near half-mile of Thames frontage, the refurbished Pier Square and the Riverside Gardens give the area a distinctive waterside draw across the year.

The leisure and activity layer reaches along the river and into the green spaces. Lesnes Abbey Woods, with the ruins of the abbey founded in 1178 set in woodland and heathland famous for its spring bluebells and its fossil beds, give walkers and families a major draw, while Erith Marshes and the riverside paths of the Thames offer wide open walking. The London Loop and the Green Chain Walk both run through, keeping activity operators and day-out trade busy through the warmer season.

Heritage and culture run deep here. Hall Place and Gardens, the Tudor mansion of around 1537 set in award-winning gardens on the River Cray nearby, anchors the borough's heritage offer with its house, topiary and grounds, while the medieval Church of St John the Baptist and the conservation streets of old Erith add depth. The annual Erith Riverside Festival, the events at Riverside Gardens and the wider Bexley heritage calendar fill the diary across the season.

Underpinning it all is a hotel and serviced-stay trade serving riverside business, day-trippers and visitors heading into the capital, with a guide and day-out scene built around the pier, Lesnes Abbey and Hall Place. Erith station on the North Kent line links the town to London and along the river to Dartford and Woolwich, and the road network and river crossings carry visitors in, so operators handle stopover trade as well as day-trippers heading along the wider Thames riverside nearby.
